name: Podcast Production
description: Persian-language podcast production brings together research, writing, narration, sound design, visual identity, and digital publication. Channel B and BPlus illustrate distinct approaches to narrative nonfiction and book-based audio, without representing the entire Iranian podcast sector.

seo.title: Podcast Production in Iran and Persian-Language Media | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore Persian-language podcast production through documented examples of research, narration, sound design, supporting publications, and distribution.

content.heading: An editorial medium built for listening
content.content:
Persian-language podcasts offer a useful way to explore Iranian content production, but language and production location must be kept separate. A Persian programme can address listeners across borders; its language alone does not establish where its staff work or where its audience lives. The examples here therefore describe documented production practices rather than a geographically complete industry. Channel B presents true stories in narrated audio, while BPlus describes its podcast as a way to introduce books and their principal ideas. These are different editorial propositions, even when they share people or audiences. [s1][s3]

For an international reader, the distinction matters: a podcast made for Persian-speaking listeners need not be about Iran. Channel B’s published catalogue includes stories about Watergate, Antarctic exploration, and the Lufthansa robbery. Its cultural significance includes making subjects available through Persian narration, rather than simply documenting domestic events. [s2]

content.heading: The work behind a recognisable voice
content.content:
Channel B dates its beginnings to summer 1394 in the Iranian Solar Hijri calendar, initially with assistance from Namlik, an audio platform. Its account describes a project that developed into a team as the material and production work became more extensive. [s1]

The team page makes the division of labour unusually visible. Ali Bandari is identified as the originating producer and the voice listeners hear. Omid Sedighfar’s role includes editing raw speech, selecting music, and arranging the audio narrative. Other credited responsibilities include original music, episode posters, executive coordination, website development, publication, and finances. This is evidence of a particular team’s organisation, rather than a staffing template that every Iranian podcast follows. [s1]

The resulting lesson is practical: the apparent intimacy of a narrator speaking directly to a listener can rest on a much wider production effort. Artwork and a maintained website also belong to that effort, even though neither is audible in an episode. [s1]

content.heading: Research extends beyond the audio file
content.content:
Channel B’s supporting page for its Watergate series lists websites, books, interviews, documentary material, and recorded audio. The bibliography includes journalism alongside archival and institutional resources. This establishes that the producers disclose a research trail; it does not independently verify every claim made in the finished programme. A listener investigating a particular assertion would still need to examine the relevant underlying source. [s4]

Such supporting publications also reveal how an audio story can have a second life as written material. A bibliography helps listeners distinguish the programme’s synthesis from its inputs and gives them routes into further reading. It is especially useful when a narrative draws on sources in another language. These are editorial implications of the published source list, rather than measured findings about listener behaviour. [s4]

content.heading: Format, access, and reuse
content.content:
BPlus distinguishes its book-summary podcast from its YouTube work on history, ideas, and the phenomena that shaped the world. The distinction shows why an audio episode and a video from the same editorial project should not automatically be treated as interchangeable products. Their stated purposes differ. [s3]

Both BPlus and Channel B state that their podcast episodes are free to hear, while requiring permission for republication. Free listening therefore does not establish an unrestricted right to copy a recording or reproduce its text. [s1][s3]

These examples illuminate craft and editorial organisation more securely than market scale. They show the importance of a clear premise, credited production roles, and supporting material. They do not establish national listening totals, typical production budgets, or the financial sustainability of Persian-language podcasting. [s1][s3][s4]

name: Commercial Photography
description: Commercial photography in Iran includes commissioned images of products, food, fashion, architecture, and industrial activity. Selected studio portfolios show photography operating alongside video, campaign planning, and social media production, with documented examples in Tehran and Mashhad.

seo.title: Commercial Photography in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Iranian commercial photography through documented product, food, fashion, architectural, and industrial studio portfolios.

content.heading: Images commissioned to communicate
content.content:
Commercial photography is best understood here through its commissioned purpose: presenting a product, place, service, or brand to an intended audience. Iranian studio portfolios reveal a broad field rather than a single visual style. Bartstudio separates architectural, industrial, advertising, restaurant, jewellery, portrait, and fashion work. SPIN describes product, architectural, spatial, and brand-oriented portrait photography. These categories identify different subjects and client needs; they are not interchangeable labels for attractive pictures. [s1][s2]

The sources also show why commercial photography belongs within content production. A photograph may be one component of a larger campaign involving moving images, copy, and publication. Reihanet Studio explicitly offers photography alongside video editing, campaign concepts, and social media management. Its service description documents an integrated offering, although it does not establish that every Iranian photographer works within an agency. [s3]

content.heading: From a factory floor to a restaurant table
content.content:
Bartstudio identifies itself as the joint practice of Ashkan Ghafari and Yasaman Khosravi, active in Tehran since 2018. Its portfolio includes industrial and mining work as well as architecture and advertising. This range makes an important distinction visible: commercial image-making is not confined to consumer fashion or small objects photographed in a studio. Buildings, production environments, and business facilities can also be commissioned subjects. [s1]

SPIN provides a different view from Mashhad, a major city in northeastern Iran. Its photography portfolio names restaurant, catering, confectionery, and food-business projects, including work explicitly labelled for social media and Instagram. These examples establish activity outside the capital without supporting a ranking of cities or a claim about regional market shares. They also show that a local hospitality business can be a commercial photography client alongside larger brands. [s2]

content.heading: A photograph within a campaign
content.content:
Reihanet’s archive gives concrete examples of how subjects and outputs overlap. It describes fashion collection photography and campaign video for Adora, food photography and videography for Patiss Cafe Bakery, and advertising images of Alborz Ceramic tiles arranged on stairs and in still-life settings. These project descriptions show different ways of presenting goods: on a person, within a usable environment, or as part of a composed scene. [s3]

The same studio groups its services into production, campaigns, and account management. Its descriptions include concepts developed with the client before shooting, followed by content creation and publication-related work. The editorial implication is that evaluating a commercial image requires attention to its intended use as well as its appearance. A striking individual frame and a coherent sequence for a brand’s feed solve related but distinct communication problems. This interpretation follows the studio’s service structure; it is not evidence of campaign effectiveness. [s3]

content.heading: What a portfolio can establish
content.content:
A portfolio is valuable primary evidence of the work a studio chooses to present and the services it says it supplies. It is weaker evidence for typical prices, independently confirmed client satisfaction, or business outcomes. SPIN’s statements about conveying brand messages and Bartstudio’s service categories should therefore be read as professional self-descriptions rather than independent performance assessments. [s1][s2]

Taken together, the examples reveal a varied commissioned practice spanning food businesses, built environments, industry, and consumer brands. They also caution against treating commercial photography as a synonym for documentary reporting: these portfolios organise images around client communication. The clearest reading of the field starts with the subject, the commission, and the intended publication context, while keeping claims about sales impact or national scale separate from the available evidence. [s1][s2][s3]

name: Digital Illustration
description: Digital illustration connects drawing and visual storytelling with computer-based image creation. Iranian examples include blended pencil and digital painting, concept art for entertainment, and diaspora practices that reinterpret cultural references through digital images.

seo.title: Digital Illustration in Iran and Its Diaspora | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore Iranian digital illustration through documented approaches to pencil and digital painting, concept art, visual storytelling, and cultural references.

content.heading: A method that crosses artistic boundaries
content.content:
Digital illustration does not describe a single Iranian aesthetic. The examples examined here range from a Tehran illustrator blending pencil drawing with digital painting to an Iran-based concept artist using both digital and traditional sketches. A further example comes from an Iranian-British artist working in London. Together they show why medium, subject, and location should be considered separately: Iranian cultural connections do not necessarily imply residence in Iran, and computer-based production does not imply a uniform appearance. [s1][s2][s3]

The boundary between handwork and digital work is particularly important. Ghazal Fatollahi’s account of combining pencil and digital painting makes it inappropriate to describe all such images as created entirely on a computer. Likewise, Reza Afshar’s stated use of both kinds of sketching suggests continuity in drawing practice across tools rather than a simple replacement of one medium by another. [s1][s2]

content.heading: Illustration as an extension of a story
content.content:
Fatollahi describes a path from graphic-design study and a university project on children’s and young-adult book illustration into publishing. Her biography identifies geometric organisation, patterned surfaces, and perspectives compared with cinematic scenes as characteristics of her work. It also connects some motifs to Persian carpets and Iranian architecture. These are descriptions of one artist’s practice, not a definition of Iranian illustration as a whole. [s1]

Her stated aim is for illustrations to extend and narrate a text. That offers a useful distinction between illustration and simple ornament: an image can contribute its own information, viewpoint, or sequence to a reader’s encounter with a story. In this example, digital painting participates in a broader narrative practice grounded in drawing and page design. The source does not identify the production technique of every individual book, so the mixed technique should not be assigned indiscriminately to her entire bibliography. [s1]

content.heading: Concept art and imagined worlds
content.content:
KAFT’s designer profile presents Reza Afshar as an illustrator and concept artist whose work spans video games, films, cover art, and animation. Concept art here refers to the visual development of imagined characters, settings, or worlds for a larger creative project. The profile links his interests to fiction, novels, and games, rather than limiting his imagery to explicitly Iranian subjects. [s2]

Afshar describes frequent sketching with both traditional and digital techniques, allowing a story to emerge through the act of drawing. This account foregrounds exploration: a sketch can be a way to discover an idea before it becomes a finished image. The profile supports discussion of his stated process and professional fields, but it does not provide a verified client-by-client production history or a measure of Iran’s games-art workforce. [s2]

content.heading: Cultural references without a single national style
content.content:
Sina Hafezi, who identifies himself as an Iranian-British digital artist, describes a different route into image-making. His account connects music and imagined moving illustrations with learning to realise images digitally, initially producing canvas prints for his home. He describes separate Iran and international collections, with calligraphy among the influences entering some work. He also explicitly describes digital art as a pursuit alongside his professional work in science and engineering. [s3]

This example broadens the picture beyond full-time commercial illustration while keeping the geographic distinction clear: it is a diaspora practice, not evidence of a studio operating inside Iran. Read together, the three accounts show cultural inheritance, narrative ambition, and digital technique combining in different ways. They support an understanding of illustration through individual processes and uses; they do not justify a single national style, a standard career path, or an estimate of the sector’s economic size. [s1][s2][s3]
